options: Shake it out well so the dust is removed first

Put it on the clean linen shelf until it is washed

options: It goes into the normal linen bag with the rest

essays.stem: Describe how you would collect and check a guest's laundry before it is washed.
essays.modelAnswer: I collect the laundry bag from the room, or from the guest, at the time the property says, and I check that the laundry list is filled in with the guest's name, room number, the service wanted (normal or express) and the number of each item. In the laundry I count every item against the list. If the count is different, I note it and tell the guest or my supervisor before anything is washed. I check every pocket and remove pens, tissues, coins, money, jewellery and phones; I record anything valuable and return it as the rules say. I look at each item for stains, tears, missing buttons or faded colour, and I note them on the list so the guest is not blamed on us, and I tell the guest of any damage first. I read the care labels and set aside anything that must be dry cleaned or hand washed. I tag each item, or bag it, with the room number so it does not get mixed with other guests' clothes.
markingPoints: Checks the list: name, room, service and item count
Counts the items and reports any difference before washing
Empties pockets and records valuables
Notes stains and damage and tells the guest first
Reads care labels and tags items with the room number

essays.stem: Explain how to sort laundry before washing, and why each step matters.
essays.modelAnswer: I sort laundry so that each item gets the right wash and nothing is spoiled. First I keep each guest's items together and tagged, so they do not get mixed up. I read the care label on every item. I sort by colour: whites, light colours and dark colours are washed apart, because dyes can run and stain lighter items. New dark items are washed alone the first time. I sort by fabric and care: cotton and linen can take hot washes, synthetics need a cooler wash, and wool, silk and lace need a gentle or hand wash, or a mesh bag. Items marked dry clean only are set aside. I sort by how dirty items are: heavily soiled kitchen cloths or pool towels are not washed with guest shirts. Items with stains are pre-treated first. Soiled or contaminated linen is kept apart and washed as the property's rules say. Sorting this way stops colour runs, shrinking and damage, and gives a cleaner wash.
markingPoints: Keeps each guest's items together and reads care labels
Sorts by colour to stop dyes running; new darks alone
Sorts by fabric and care, setting aside dry clean and delicate items
Sorts by soil level and pre-treats stains
Keeps contaminated linen apart and explains the purpose of sorting

essays.stem: Explain the five main care label symbols and what each one tells you.
essays.modelAnswer: Care labels use five main symbols. The washtub is about washing. A number inside it is the highest water temperature in degrees Celsius, or dots are used, with more dots meaning hotter. A hand in the tub means hand wash only, and lines under the tub mean a gentler cycle. The triangle is about bleach. An empty triangle means any bleach may be used, a triangle with two slanted lines means only non-chlorine bleach, and a crossed triangle means no bleach. The square is about drying. A square with a circle inside means it can be tumble dried, with dots for the heat; other lines in a square show line drying or drying flat. The iron is about ironing, and its dots show the heat: one dot cool, two dots warm, three dots hot. The circle is about dry cleaning, and a letter inside tells the cleaner which method to use. Any symbol with a cross through it means do not do that process.
markingPoints: Washtub: temperature by number or dots; hand wash; gentle cycle lines
Triangle: bleach, including non-chlorine and no bleach
Square: drying, including tumble dry with heat dots
Iron: heat shown by one to three dots
Circle: dry cleaning; a cross means do not

essays.stem: Describe how to wash a load of white cotton bath towels, from loading the machine to unloading it.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the towels are all white cotton and read a care label to confirm the wash temperature and whether bleach is allowed. I shake out sand from beach or pool towels outside, gently, and pre-treat any stains, such as make-up or sunscreen, with a suitable product. I check the machine is clean and the filters are clear. I load the towels loosely, up to the weight the maker gives and no more, so they can move and get clean. I wear gloves and measure the detergent as the label says for the load size, how dirty it is and the water, using the machine's dispenser or dosing system. If the care label and the property's rules allow, I add bleach only in its own dispenser, never mixed with other products. I choose a hot cotton programme as the label allows, so the towels are clean and hygienic. When the cycle ends I unload promptly so they do not smell, take them out a few at a time into a clean trolley, and check them for stains or damage before drying.
markingPoints: Checks fabric and care label; removes sand and pre-treats stains
Loads loosely to the maker's capacity
Measures detergent as the label says, with gloves; bleach only if allowed and never mixed
Chooses a suitable hot cotton programme
Unloads promptly into a clean trolley and checks for stains or damage

essays.stem: Describe how to use a tumble dryer safely, including the fire risks.
essays.modelAnswer: Before each load I clean the lint filter, because lint is very flammable and a blocked filter makes the dryer overheat. I check the care labels and only tumble dry items that allow it, choosing the heat the label shows. I do not overload the dryer, so air can move and items dry evenly. Items that have had oil on them, such as spa massage towels, kitchen cloths or towels with sunscreen, must be washed well first, because oil left in fabric can heat up by itself after drying and catch fire. These items are dried on a lower heat, and the dryer is always allowed to finish its cool-down part of the cycle. I never stop a dryer early and leave hot items piled up; if I must, I take them out at once and spread them out to cool. I never dry items with rubber or foam backing unless the label allows. I never leave a dryer running when the laundry is closed. I keep the area round the dryer clear, and I know where the fire extinguisher is.
markingPoints: Cleans the lint filter every load and explains why
Follows care labels and does not overload
Explains the oily fabric risk and washes oily items well first
Lets the cool-down finish; never piles hot items
Never leaves the dryer running unattended; keeps the area clear and knows the extinguisher

essays.stem: Describe how to iron a guest's cotton shirt and get it ready to return.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the care label and set the iron to the right heat for cotton, testing it on a hidden part first, such as the inside of the tail. I use steam or a slightly damp shirt, because cotton presses better a little damp. I iron in a set order so I do not crease the parts already done. I start with the collar, ironing the underside first and then the top, from the points to the middle. Next I do the cuffs, inside then outside, then the sleeves, laid flat along the seam, front and back. Then I do the shoulders or yoke over the narrow end of the board, then the back, and last the two front panels, ironing carefully round the buttons, never over them. I hang the shirt on a hanger at once and do up the top and middle buttons so it keeps its shape. I check it for creases and marks, and I fold or hang it as the guest asked. I never leave the iron face down, and I stand it upright when I put it down.
markingPoints: Checks the label, sets the heat and tests on a hidden part
Uses steam or a slightly damp shirt
Correct order: collar, cuffs, sleeves, yoke, back, fronts
Irons round buttons, hangs and buttons the shirt at once and checks it
Uses the iron safely: never face down, stood upright

essays.stem: Explain how to return a guest's laundry, and how you would deal with a complaint that an item is missing or damaged.
essays.modelAnswer: Before returning the laundry I check every item against the laundry list, make sure each one is clean, pressed and folded or hung as asked, and put the room number on the package. I make sure the charge from the list is recorded so it can be added to the room bill. I deliver it at the time promised. I knock and announce myself, and give it to the guest, or if the guest is out, I place it in the room as the property's rules say, never leaving it in the corridor. If a guest complains that an item is missing or damaged, I listen without arguing, say sorry for the trouble, and write down the details. I do not blame the guest or make promises I cannot keep. I check the laundry list, the notes made at collection, the laundry room, and other guests' bags in case it was mixed up. I tell my supervisor at once, because they decide on any refund or replacement, and I make sure the guest is told what is happening.
markingPoints: Checks items against the list and presents them as asked
Records the charge for the room bill
Delivers on time and follows the rules if the guest is out
Listens, says sorry and records details without arguing or blaming
Searches, checks the collection notes and tells the supervisor, keeping the guest informed

essays.stem: Explain how to handle soiled and contaminated linen hygienically.
essays.modelAnswer: Used linen carries germs, so I wear gloves when I handle it, and an apron for heavily soiled items. I do not shake dirty linen, because that spreads dust and germs into the air. I roll it up with the dirty side inside and carry it away from my body, then put it straight into the dirty linen bag or trolley, never on the floor or with clean linen. Linen with blood, vomit or other body fluids is contaminated. It is put into a separate, marked bag, as the property's rules say, and taken to the laundry without being sorted by hand. It is washed apart on the hottest wash the fabric allows, or as the rules say. I keep clean and dirty linen in separate areas and trolleys, and I clean dirty linen trolleys often. I take off my gloves the right way, put them in the bin, and wash my hands well. Any needles or sharp items found in linen are not picked up by hand but reported for the sharps box.
markingPoints: Wears gloves and does not shake dirty linen
Rolls it and carries it away from the body into the dirty linen bag
Bags contaminated linen separately, marked, and washes it hot as the rules say
Keeps clean and dirty linen and trolleys apart
Removes gloves correctly, washes hands and deals with sharps safely

essays.stem: Explain the main safety hazards in a laundry and how to work safely.
essays.modelAnswer: Laundry chemicals, such as detergent, bleach and stain removers, can burn skin and eyes. I read the label and SDS, wear gloves and eye protection when measuring, use the dispensers, never mix products such as bleach and ammonia, and keep chemicals closed, labelled and stored safely. If chemical gets in an eye I rinse it with plenty of clean water and get help. Heat is another hazard. Irons, presses, dryer drums and steam can burn, so I keep my hands clear, stand irons upright and switch them off after use. Machines are dangerous too. I keep the guards on, never reach into a moving washer or a flatwork ironer, tie back long hair and remove loose jewellery. Wet laundry is heavy, so I unload a little at a time into a trolley and bend my knees. Wet floors and spilled powder are slippery, so I clean them at once and use wet floor signs. I check plugs and cables, and I clean lint filters to stop fires.
markingPoints: Chemicals: label and SDS, PPE, dispensers, never mix, eye first aid
Heat and steam: keep clear, stand irons upright, switch off
Machines: guards on, never reach in, hair tied back, no loose jewellery
Manual handling of wet laundry with a trolley and bent knees
Slips, electrical checks and lint fire risk

essays.stem: Explain how a villa or hotel controls its linen stock.
essays.modelAnswer: Linen is expensive, so it is controlled carefully. The property sets a par level, the number of full sets kept for each bed or bathroom. With a par of three, for example, one set is in use, one is in the laundry and one is clean on the shelf, and more may be kept for busy times. Dirty linen is counted when it goes to the laundry and clean linen is counted when it comes back, so missing items are found quickly. Clean linen is stored on clean shelves, off the floor, in a dry, aired linen room away from damp and insects, with the same items stacked together and folded the same way. Older stock is used first so wear is even. Each item is checked after washing; linen that is torn, thin or has stains that will not come out is taken out as a reject, recorded, and used as rags or thrown away as the rules say. Regular stock counts show how much is lost or worn, so new linen can be ordered in time.
markingPoints: Explains par levels with an example
Counts dirty linen out and clean linen back
Stores clean linen correctly and rotates stock
Checks for rejects, records and removes them
Regular stock counts to find losses and reorder in time

practical1.title: Sort, pre-treat, wash and dry a load of villa laundry
practical1.brief: As a group, process a mixed bag of villa laundry in the Centre's laundry room or the mock villa's laundry, using a washing machine and a tumble dryer. The assessor gives you a bag of bed linen, towels, a beach towel that may run, and a few clothes with care labels, some with made-up stains. Work in these stages: (1) check and count the items and empty any pockets; (2) read each care label and sort by colour, fabric and how dirty it is, writing your sort on a sheet; (3) pre-treat the stains with a suitable product; (4) check the machine, load one wash to the maker's capacity and measure the detergent; (5) choose and run the right programme; (6) unload promptly, check the items, and dry them as each label says, cleaning the lint filter first, or line dry in the shade; (7) fold the dry items the same way and stack them; (8) clean the filter and the machines and tidy the laundry. Every member sorts part of the load, reads labels aloud for the assessor, and takes part in loading, drying and folding. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A bag of mixed villa laundry with care labels, supplied by the assessor
Washing machine and tumble dryer, with the maker's instructions
Laundry detergent and a stain remover, with labels and SDS, and a measuring cup
Laundry baskets or trolleys for clean and dirty items
Clothes line and pegs (for shade drying)
A phone or camera for the photos
photos: The items counted and the pockets emptied
The sorted piles, with the sorting sheet
The machine loaded to capacity and the measured detergent
The lint filter cleaned before drying
The laundry room tidy, with machines and filters clean
checklist: Counted the items and checked every pocket
Read the care labels correctly and explained the symbols
Sorted by colour, fabric and soil, with the running item kept apart
Pre-treated stains with a suitable product, tested first
Loaded to the maker's capacity and measured the detergent with gloves on
Chose a programme that suits the care labels
Cleaned the lint filter and dried each item as its label allows
Folded items neatly and the same way
Cleaned up, worked safely and took a full part in the group
safety: Read labels and the SDS, wear gloves and eye protection when measuring, and never mix products; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Never open a machine while it is running or reach into a turning drum
Clean the lint filter before every dryer load, and do not pile up hot laundry
Unload wet laundry a little at a time into a trolley, bending the knees
Wipe up water and spilled powder at once

practical2.title: Process a guest laundry order: check, press, fold and return
practical2.brief: As a group, process a guest's laundry order for the Centre's mock villa. The assessor gives you a guest laundry bag with a laundry list and a price list in J$, and has set some tests in it (for example, a count that does not match the list, a coin in a pocket, a stain and a missing button). The washing is already done. Work in these stages: (1) check the list and count the items, and record any differences, items found and damage on the list; (2) tell the assessor (as the supervisor) about the problems, as you would before processing; (3) iron and finish a cotton shirt in the right order, testing the heat first; (4) press a pair of trousers with a crease, and iron a dark item inside out; (5) fold the towels, a flat sheet and the other items the same way; (6) package the order with the room number, check every item against the list, and work out the charge on the list before tax; (7) deliver it to the mock villa room, knocking and announcing, and explain the order to the assessor, who plays the guest. Every member irons or presses at least one item while the assessor watches, and each member checks one part of the list. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A guest laundry bag with a laundry list and a J$ price list, supplied by the assessor
Ironing boards, steam irons and a pressing cloth
Hangers, shirt bags or tissue, and laundry bags or boxes
A phone or camera for the photos
photos: The laundry list checked against the items, with differences marked
The items found in pockets and the damage noted
The shirt being ironed, with the collar and cuffs done first
The finished shirt on a hanger and the pressed trousers
The packaged order with the room number and the list showing the total
The delivery to the mock villa room
checklist: Counted the items and recorded differences, items found and damage correctly
Reported problems to the supervisor before going on
Tested the iron heat for the fabric before ironing
Ironed the shirt in the correct order with no creases or shine marks
Pressed trousers neatly and ironed the dark item inside out
Folded items neatly and the same way
Checked the package against the list and worked out the charge correctly
Delivered politely and explained the order clearly
Used the iron safely and took a full part in the group
safety: Stand the iron upright or switch it off when not in use; never leave it face down
